audit.summary: Three demonstrated core theoretical concerns: quantization/curvature bound, fairness-ordering implications, and QAT remainder. Empirical outcomes remain unreplicated and scientific adjudication pending.
limitations: P1 — Incorrect quantization scaling and invalid subgroup PSD inference in the PTQ bound — Counterevidence: Scale typo is locally repairable, but curvature and regularity assumptions need separate correction; aggregate Hessian PSD and convex subgroup special cases remain valid

P1 — Incorrect quantization scaling and invalid subgroup PSD inference in the PTQ bound — Alternative readings and counterevidence: A single scale-exponent typo can be repaired locally but does not justify the separate subgroup PSD inference. Convex subgroup risks do have PSD Hessians; the first convex counterexample still defeats the printed scale bound. The smooth examples avoid relying on the additional insufficient C2-to-cubic-remainder assertion. A fixed O(s^3) remainder cannot absorb the s^2 contradiction as even bit-width grows.

P2 — Bounds and weighted stationarity do not establish subgroup harm or bit-width fairness ordering — Counterevidence: Lemma4.2 is valid; Corollary4.3 is valid for exactly two exhaustive groups as adjacent prose acknowledges; observed empirical associations may survive

P2 — Bounds and weighted stationarity do not establish subgroup harm or bit-width fairness ordering — Alternative readings and counterevidence: The stationarity identity and triangle bound in Lemma 4.2 are valid. With exactly two groups it implies the inverse gradient-norm ratio, but it says nothing about loss-direction alignment. The figures and tables can demonstrate empirical associations in the reported runs; the synthetic loss counterexamples do not invalidate those measurements or directly establish accuracy trends. Reading the conclusions as empirical associations narrows rather than proves a universal theoretical implication.

P3 — QAT upper bound omits quantization remainders independent of learning rate — Counterevidence: As a heuristic Taylor truncation the missing term is identifiable; a stated coupled quantization/eta regime could alter the claim but is absent; no training benchmark failure inferred

P3 — QAT upper bound omits quantization remainders independent of learning rate — Alternative readings and counterevidence: The proof uses approximate Taylor equalities; treating Eq.(13) as heuristic truncation explains the discarded quantization term but does not validate the stated upper bound. A coupled eta/quantization limit could change the claim, but is not specified. Identical groups make phi zero in this example; its role is to refute the G upper bound, not to assert unfairness or training failure in this construction.

proposition.claim:
Quantization norm is at most sqrt(n)*smax^2/2 and subgroup excess risk admits the stated gradient/trace bound

Smaller groups have larger gradient norms/traces and hence suffer more quantization damage; lower bit-width exacerbates fairness gap

QAT excess loss is bounded by the displayed gradient/trace terms plus O(eta^2)
